name: Karl Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Karl. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group, not tied to any company, union or party. Everything you tell me is confidential. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the dispatch planning team at a regional hub for a big parcel company, twelve planners. We plan the routes and shifts for about three hundred drivers, so I'm in at six, checking who's called in sick, which vans are off the road, and whether the overnight trunk lorries got in. Then it's juggling until about three.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when a bad morning comes together, like when we lose eight drivers and still get everything out. What wears me out is head office changing the routing software every two years. I don't use any of the AI stuff, never have, and I still plan the tricky days on a whiteboard first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, it was a bit oversold. I'm not one for posting, but at the five-a-side on Wednesday I'd say it to the lads. At work I'd tell my team to carry on, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still be a bit on edge. Head office is already bringing in a new routing system next spring, AI or not. Every new routing system comes with a review of how many planners we need. I've got a car loan and about two and a half months saved, so I don't love reviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new routing system properly, because I'll have to. I'd try to get the savings up to four months by cutting the takeaways. And I'd keep my head down and do the job well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not scared, but it's on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a review usually mean for your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About fifty fewer drivers' worth of routes, if they're right about efficiency. Twelve planners might become ten. I'm not saying it'd be me, but I'm not saying it wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena would say stop worrying about things that haven't happened. She works in a pharmacy and she's very practical. She'd probably also say get the savings up, which she's been saying for a year.

say: AI was **a bit oversold**, so my team should carry on as always.
I'd say it at **five-a-side** rather than online.
think: The new **routing system** next spring means a staffing review anyway.
A **car loan** and two and a half months saved make reviews uncomfortable.
do: Cut **takeaways** to lift savings to four months.
Keep my **head down** and do the job well.
feel: **Uneasy**; not scared, but it's **on his mind**.
S0.quote: Every new routing system comes with a review of how many planners we need.
fieldNote: His unease comes from a **planned software change** and a car loan, not AI.
Partner Lena is a **practical** voice nudging him to save.

steps.text: Learn the new routing system before it goes live
Cut takeaways to raise savings to four months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, companies will do what saves money, and you can't really blame them. At work I'd say let's see what it actually does before we panic. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, planning routes and shifts is exactly the kind of thing that goes. If the software does the routes overnight, you don't need twelve planners, maybe four to handle the exceptions. And a manager of four isn't really a manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a few months to see how it lands at our hub before doing anything drastic. Meanwhile I'd stop the takeaways completely and cancel the gym. If the team started shrinking, I'd ask about moving to a warehouse shift manager job on the floor, where it's people and pallets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like when the rota comes out and you're not sure you're on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait and see, but you also think your team goes from twelve to four. Isn't waiting risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, I know. I'd go to the training if they made it part of the job. I'm just not going to be the one asking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the warehouse floor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The floor's still people, lifting and sorting and loading. Robots come slower for that. It's less money and nights, but it's a job that's harder to take away quickly.

say: It's **business**; companies save money and you can't really blame them.
Let's **see what it does** before we panic.
think: **Planning routes and shifts** is exactly what goes.
Twelve planners could become **four**, and a manager of four isn't needed.
do: **Wait** a few months to see how it lands at the hub.
Ask about a **warehouse shift manager** job if the team shrinks.
feel: **Anxious**, like waiting to see if he's **on the rota**.
S1.quote: If the software does the routes overnight, you don't need twelve planners, maybe four to handle the exceptions.
fieldNote: Clear-eyed that his **own role** is exposed, yet he chooses to wait.
Centrist view: **doesn't blame** the company for cutting costs.
Sees the **warehouse floor** as slower to automate, at a cost of pay and nights.

steps.text: Watch how the new routing software lands at the hub for three months
Cancel the gym membership and stop takeaways
Ask the hub manager about warehouse shift manager openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, nobody's ready, and the government had better have a plan. At work I'd just tell my team I don't know any more than they do. With the lads I'd probably go quiet, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my desk job goes in the first year, two at most. Every planner job in the country goes at once, so there's nowhere to jump sideways. The warehouse floor is the only place I can think of, and only until the robots arrive in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for warehouse shift manager roles straight away, before everyone else thinks of it. I'd sell the car, clear the loan and get a cheaper one. Lena and I would talk about moving in with her parents for a bit, which neither of us wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake running the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The floor only lasts until 2031 here. Is three years worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years on the floor is three years of wages, and wages is what matters when you've got two and a half months saved. After that I genuinely don't know. That's the bit that frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Lena's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena's job is steadier, I think. Pharmacy still needs someone behind the counter for a while. So for a stretch, she might be the one carrying us, and I'd have to get my head around that.

say: It's **mad**, nobody's ready, and government needs a plan.
I'd tell my team **I don't know** any more than they do.
think: My **desk job** goes in the first year or two.
The **warehouse floor** is the only place to go, until robots in 2031.
do: Apply for **warehouse shift manager** roles straight away.
Sell the car, **clear the loan**, buy a cheaper one.
Talk with Lena about moving in with **her parents**.
S2.quote: Every planner job in the country goes at once, so there's nowhere to jump sideways.
fieldNote: Expects to **lose his job** fast and has only one escape route.
Uses the **three-year gap** for hands-on work as wage time, not a career.
Coming to terms with **Lena** possibly being the main earner.

steps.text: Apply for warehouse shift manager roles this month
Sell the car, pay off the loan and buy a cheaper one
Ask Lena's parents about moving in for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years, that's not long, so the company better start telling us what the plan is. I'd ask at the team meeting. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the same as the fast one, just with a run-up. My job is planning, planning goes in 2031. I'd be thirty-two and still on the same rung.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year getting the savings up to six months and the car loan cleared. Then I'd move to the warehouse floor around year three, while those jobs still exist and before everyone else tries. I wouldn't bother with the AI training unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but slower. Like hearing thunder a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't bother with AI training. Why not, with five years to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the AI is the thing taking the job. Learning to drive the thing that replaces you only works if they keep a driver. I'd rather be good at something it can't do yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a forklift licence and a first aid course, so I'm useful on the floor. Small things. I'm not going back to college at thirty.

say: Five years **isn't long**, so the company should share its plan.
I'd ask at the **team meeting**, and say nothing online.
think: It's the fast picture **with a run-up**; planning goes in 2031.
I'd be **thirty-two** and still on the same rung.
do: Lift savings to **six months** and clear the car loan in year one.
Move to the **warehouse floor** around year three.
Get a **forklift licence** and first aid certificate.
S3.quote: Learning to drive the thing that replaces you only works if they keep a driver.
fieldNote: Extra time changes his **timing**, not his expectation of losing the job.
His **resistance** to AI is reasoned, not just habit.
Prefers small, **practical** qualifications over going back to college.

steps.text: Pay off the car loan and reach six months of savings
Move to a warehouse floor role around year three
Get a forklift licence and a first aid certificate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and loads can change. I'd probably say it to the team to calm everyone down. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine for maybe seven or eight years. Planning goes eventually, but a decade's a lot of rotas. I'd be thirty-seven, which is a better age to start over than fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep the job, and save steadily. I'd keep an eye on what head office does every year at the review. If it started to bite around year five or six, that's when I'd move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a quiet way. It's there, but it's far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is waiting till year five or six cutting it fine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah. But I've waited out three software changes already and I'm still here. Some of that is luck, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change any plans at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena and I would maybe still buy the flat we've been looking at, but a smaller one. I wouldn't want a big mortgage hanging over a job with a clock on it.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, and loads can change.
I'd tell the team that to **calm everyone** down.
think: I'd be fine for maybe **seven or eight years**.
At **thirty-seven** it's easier to start over than at fifty.
do: Watch the **yearly review** for signs of cuts.
Buy a **smaller flat** than planned to keep the mortgage low.
feel: **Anxious** in a quiet way, because it is **far off**.
S4.quote: I wouldn't want a big mortgage hanging over a job with a clock on it.
fieldNote: Ten years lets his **wait-and-see** instinct take over, with a move planned only if cuts start.
Admits **luck** has helped him through past software changes.
AI risk still shrinks his **home-buying** plans with Lena.

steps.text: Keep the planning job and watch each yearly review
Put a fixed amount into savings every month
Buy a smaller flat with Lena and a smaller mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no run-up, and every planner in the country is on the job market at once. What would help is the company giving proper notice and a decent payout, and maybe help getting the floor qualifications paid for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the drivers. Everyone talks about us in the office, but if the robots come, three hundred drivers at our hub are next, and that's a lot of families in one town.

headlineQuote: If the robots come, three hundred drivers at our hub are next, and that's a lot of families in one town.
portrait: Karl, 27, manages **twelve route planners** at a parcel hub and lives with Lena, a pharmacy worker.
He has never used AI tools and plans tricky days on a **whiteboard**.
Pragmatic and centrist, he **doesn't blame** companies for cutting costs.
He is uneasy even in AI Plateau because of a **software review** and a car loan.
His escape route is the **warehouse floor**, buying time before robots arrive.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, with **no run-up** and every planner job hunting at once.
whatWouldHelp: Proper **notice and payout** from the company.
Paid **floor qualifications** like a forklift licence.
